analysis.one_liner: Restores stricter federal oversight of banks and financial firms between $10 billion and $250 billion in assets.
analysis.headline: The bill to re-tighten bank oversight after the 2018 rollback was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal a 2018 law that freed mid-sized banks and nonbank financial companies from strict federal rules. It would lower the asset thresholds at which firms must pass stress tests, hold more liquid assets, limit borrowing, file living wills for unwinding without a bailout, and maintain risk committees. This restores oversight that applied before 2018 to banks like the ones that failed or needed rescue in 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank customers and taxpayers benefit. Tighter stress tests and liquidity rules make mid-sized banks less likely to fail, protecting depositors from frozen accounts and the federal insurance fund from costly rescues like the ones after Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank in 2023. Resolving a failed bank under a living will, rather than emergency Fed lending, shifts the cost of failure back onto the bank's own creditors instead of the public.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lowers the threshold for mandatory enhanced prudential standards from $250 billion to $50 billion in assets, restoring stress testing, leverage limits, liquidity requirements, and resolution-plan requirements for more large firms [S2][S3].

It expands stress testing: company-run stress tests would be required starting at $10 billion in assets (down from $250 billion) and run annually or semiannually, with a third stress scenario added for board-run tests [S2].
It lowers the threshold for mandatory risk committees from $50 billion to $10 billion, so more firms must have a board-level group watching for failure risk [S2].
The bill also subjects nonbank financial companies — large financial firms without banking licenses — to the same restored oversight, closing a gap left by the 2018 rollback [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on mid-sized banks, bank holding companies, and nonbank financial companies with roughly $10–250 billion in assets, which would face compliance costs for annual stress testing, higher liquidity holdings, and limits on borrowing. Shareholders may see lower profits, and some banks argue reduced compliance burdens are what keeps smaller regional banks able to compete against Wall Street giants.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: annual and semiannual company-run stress tests plus added liquidity requirements impose recurring expenses on banks as small as $10 billion in assets, and critics of the pre-2018 rules argued these costs push regional banks toward consolidation with the very largest ones [S2].

A $10 billion threshold for stress tests and risk committees reaches well beyond the giant institutions whose 2023 failures drove this bill; community and mid-sized banks would bear testing obligations regardless of their individual risk profile [S2].

The bill is a blunt instrument: it restores the pre-2018 regime wholesale rather than tailoring requirements to a firm's risk, which is the approach the 2018 law took when it gave the Federal Reserve discretion over firms between $100 billion and $250 billion [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — making mid-sized banks less likely to fail and shifting the cost of failure off taxpayers — is substantial, as the 2023 bank failures showed what the lighter rules allowed. The costs are real but mostly fall on the firms being regulated, and the main honest objection is the low $10 billion cutoff, which sweeps in banks far smaller than the ones that actually failed. On balance the protections outweigh the compliance burden, though a tiered threshold would have targeted risk better.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when this Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Seth Moulton introduced the bill on March 14, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
No hearings, markups, amendments, or votes are recorded in the action history; the last entry is the committee referral [S5].
The bill drew zero cosponsors in the House [S4].
The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, having never reached the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mid-sized banks, large nonbank financial firms, and their shareholders are better off, because they keep the lighter 2018 rules and avoid new stress testing, liquidity, and resolution-planning costs. The House Financial Services Committee majority, which never scheduled the bill, also avoided a vote on bank regulation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mid-sized banks that avoid new rules

for.name: Rep. Seth Moulton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee, with no House cosponsors joining [S1][S4].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it [S5].

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee calendar and did not schedule the bill for any action during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the only signal is that the Democratic sponsor attracted zero cosponsors in a chamber where his party held 213 seats, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Mid-sized and regional banks ($50–250 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill would restore mandatory stress tests, liquidity requirements, leverage limits, and living-will plans these banks were freed from by the 2018 rollback, raising their compliance costs and limiting how far they can stretch their balance sheets. Their interest in keeping the lighter regime runs against depositors', since the 2023 failures of banks in this size range showed the cheaper route ends in rescues paid for by everyone else.

The bill subjects firms without banking licenses to restored oversight standards, ending the exemption the 2018 law created for them. These firms' interest in staying outside the stricter framework runs against the public's, since their failure can require a public rescue just as a bank's would.

The bill's $10 billion cutoff would require annual company-run stress tests and risk committees at banks of this size, though they would escape the full enhanced prudential standards that apply at $50 billion. They bear real testing costs while gaining only partial protection from the failure-contagion risk posed by their larger neighbors.
